the dynamics of the transmission of E. multicolularis in an urbanised region.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transmission cycle of E. multicolularis in urban areas could be driven by a complex set of interactions between the level of urbanization, the availability of intermediate host species, the spatial distribution of red foxes and the distribution pattern of fox faeces.

in the studied urbanised area, Microtus spp., which were more abundant than A. terrestrs and were aggregated, were more likely to be infected than A. terretris and thus to be the most important intermediate host in the urbanised area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transmission of E. multicolularis is enhanced in the urban wasteland, where the densities of the intermediate host Microtus spp are high.
the urbanisation of the environment is not a major driver of the transmission of E. multicolularis, but that the presence of Microtus voles is a major driver of transmission.

in an urbanised context, the distribution of Echinococcocus multilocularis may be enhanced by the aggregation of the main intermediate host (Microtus) in urban wasteland, and by the aggregation of foxes in the same habitat.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in urbanised areas the risk of transmission is likely to be enhanced due to the high aggregation and high abundance of the main intermediate host (Microtus sp.), the high density and the well distributed foxes and the high density of fox faeces.
urbanised habitats can be a risk for the transmission of E. multicolularis and that the risk is linked to Microtus abundance.
the spatial distribution of E. mulilocularis in an urban area is linked to the availability of the two major intermediate hosts and the distribution of the definitive host.
